[00:00] Okay, welcome back. In the last lecture, we looked at copilot for sales and copilot for service. Now we shift to the operation side of Dynamics 365, finance and supply chain management. These co-pilots handle some of the most tedious high volume work in enterprise operations, invoice processing, inventory management, procurement, etc.

[00:25] The exam tests your ability to design and orchestrate AI across these modules. So, Copilot for finance sits inside the finance app and automates task that accountants have done manually for decades. The headline feature is three-way invoice matching. So, an invoice arrives from a vendor and the co-pilot checks it against the purchase order and the receiving record. If all three match, auto approve. Mismatch on the quantity or the price, flag for human review. This process used to take hours per batch. Now it's seconds.

[01:05] Anomaly detection works alongside matching. If an invoice is 30% higher than normal for that vendor, Copilot flags it. It could be a price increase. It could be a typo. Could be fraud. The system catches it so that humans can investigate. Compliance checking runs every invoice against your spending rules. Is the vendor on the blacklist? Has the department exceeded its budget? The transaction exceeds authority limit.

[01:34] Copilot catches it and routes it to the right approver. At month end, C-Pilot will automate acrruel recording, identifying invoices received but not yet paid and calculating the acrrual entries. The variance analysis compares actual spending to budget highlighting exceptions so the finance teams can investigate the outliers instead of manually reviewing everything. So co-pilot for supply chain is typically more autonomous than the finance co-pilot. It continuously monitors and proactively acts. Uh so stockout prediction is the core feature here. The co-pilot analyzes demand forecast, current inventory levels, and your supplier lead times. If it predicts a stockout, like component X will run out

[02:26] next Wednesday, which halts three production lines, it alerts the team, or it can autotrigger a reorder. Quality flagging watches incoming shipments. Normal defect rate is say 2% but a shipment comes in at 8%. C-pilot will flag this immediately so you can investigate the vendor quality issue before accepting the full shipment.

[02:51] Logistics optimization consolidates shipments and optimizes carrier selection. Multiple orders going to the same region? Combine them. Tight deadline, switch to an expedited carrier. The agent balances cost and speed based on your configured priorities. Inventory monitoring tracks both ends. So slowmoving items that should be marked for clearance as well as fastmoving items where orders need to increase to be ahead of demand.

[03:23] On the exam, remember that supply chain agents are often autonomous and eventdriven. That means governance questions will focus on confidence thresholds, escalation rules, and monitoring. The real power of Dynamics 365 AI is crossmodule orchestration. Let me walk you through the scenario on screen because this is exactly the kind of design the exam will test. So let's say a customer reports a defective product.

[03:58] Step one, the service co-pilot creates a case. It verifies warranty coverage and determines a replacement is covered. Step two, a supply chain agent checks the nearest warehouse for inventory and initiates a shipment. Step three, a finance agent creates a credit memo for the customer and schedules a vendor chargeback for the defective goods. Step four, the case is updated with a tracking number and the customer is notified proactively.

[04:32] four modules, service, supply chain, finance, and then back to service all coordinating automatically. The key is that data versse is the shared backbone. When service creates the case, supply chain sees it immediately. When finance posts the credit memo, it's linked to the same case. Every audit or every handoff is logged and auditable.

[05:00] This pattern applies beyond warranty claims. Of course, a closed deal in sales can trigger finance to generate an invoice. An invoice mismatch in finance can trigger a supply chain to verify receiving records. The principle is the same. Agents in different modules react to shared data events and coordinate through data versse. The exam specifically tests whether you know that finance and operation apps support agent chat capabilities that can be extended with custom knowledge sources. So out of the box, FNO agents can answer questions about data in the system. An accounts payable clerk can ask, "Show me all the unpaid invoices over 90 days and get an answer directly in the finance app." But

[05:51] you can extend these agents with custom knowledge sources. Maybe your company has internal accounting policies that go beyond what's in data versse or uh supplier qualification procedures or compliance guidelines specific to your industry. You add these as knowledge sources and now the agent can answer questions like what's our policy for approving invoices from new vendors? and that would be grounded in your actual policy documents. You can also extend the inapp help and guidance with custom knowledge bases. When a new hire is working in the SCM app and gets stuck on how to process a return, the inapp agent can walk them through your specific procedure, not just the generic Microsoft documentation.

[06:42] The design consideration is role mapping. Say an AP clerk needs access to invoice policies and vendor management procedures. A supply chain planner needs procurement rules and logistics guidelines. Map the right knowledge sources to the right roles so that each user gets relevant contextual help. So here's your takeaways. Number one, Finance Copilot automates invoice matching, anomaly detection, and compliance all with audit trails for governance.
